entries.name: Margaret Katroscik

expected.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).
expected.sentence: Five years in federal prison, followed by five years of probation. Contemporary reporting confirms service of the prison term; exact admission and release dates remain unresolved.

updates.sentence: Five years in federal prison, followed by five years of probation. Contemporary reporting confirms service of the prison term; remanded June 5, 1970 when bail was revoked. The later prison admission and release dates remain unresolved.

entries.rationale: June 6, 1970 Associated Press report names all seven present defendants and reports Friday verdict and immediate bail revocation; absent Riddell, Quint and Muse are expressly distinguished. entries.name: Joseph E. Mulligan

expected.charges: Destruction of government property, mutilation of records, interfering with the Selective Service System, and conspiracy (the May 25, 1969 Chicago draft-record burning).
expected.sentence: Sentenced in 1970 to five years in prison followed by five years of probation for the Chicago 15 draft-record protest. Served two years at Sandstone federal prison, 1970-1972, and was released on parole in 1972. The prison admission and release months and days remain unresolved. The May 25, 1969 arrest and initial Cook County Jail detention are distinct from the later prison term; the intervening period is not treated as continuous custody.

updates.sentence: Sentenced in 1970 to five years in prison followed by five years of probation for the Chicago 15 draft-record protest. Served two years at Sandstone federal prison, 1970-1972, and was released on parole in 1972. Remanded June 5, 1970 after conviction and revocation of bail; the later Sandstone admission date and exact parole date remain unresolved. The May 25, 1969 arrest and initial Cook County Jail detention are distinct from the later prison term; the intervening period is not treated as continuous custody.
